description: A 6-core/12-thread AM5 CPU that's the go-to budget-to-midrange gaming chip right now. Pairs great with an RTX 4060/4070 without bottlenecking. Runs cool and cheap to cool with a basic AM5 stock-class cooler.

AMD's 3D V-Cache gaming flagship — still one of the best gaming CPUs you can buy thanks to its huge L3 cache. Overkill for productivity but unmatched in frame rates per rupee for pure gaming builds. Needs a B650/X670 board.

14 cores (6P+8E) that punch well above budget CPUs in both gaming and multi-threaded work like compiling or rendering. Runs hot under load, so a decent tower cooler is a must. Needs a Z-series or B760 board plus DDR5.

20-core Raptor Lake Refresh chip aimed at people who game and also do heavy multitasking, streaming, or video editing. Power-hungry — factor in a strong PSU and cooling. A step up from the i5-14600K without jumping to i9 pricing.

16-core/32-thread AM5 flagship built for serious multi-threaded work — compiling, 3D rendering, heavy ML preprocessing on CPU. More than most gamers need, but a genuine workstation-class chip. Pair with good cooling and DDR5-6000.

Entry-level ray-tracing GPU that handles 1080p (and light 1440p) gaming comfortably with DLSS 3 frame generation. Low power draw makes it easy to fit into most existing PSU setups. The safe first-dedicated-GPU pick for most builders.

A genuine 1440p powerhouse and a solid budget entry into 4K with DLSS. Sits in the sweet spot between price and performance for the current Nvidia lineup. Popular pick for anyone who also dabbles in local AI/ML workloads thanks to CUDA + decent VRAM.
High-end card built for native 4K gaming and heavier creative/AI workloads. Big generational jump over the 4070 SUPER but priced accordingly. Needs a beefy PSU (850W+) and good case airflow.

AMD's answer to the RTX 4070 — strong 1440p raster performance and more VRAM (16GB) for the price, though ray tracing trails Nvidia. Great pick if you care more about rasterized frame rates than ray tracing eye candy.

AMD's flagship with 24GB VRAM, making it attractive for 4K gaming as well as memory-hungry workloads like large AI models or video work. Ray tracing performance still lags Nvidia's equivalent tier. Needs a large case and strong PSU.

A single 16GB DDR5 stick — the baseline for a modern build, but pair two for dual-channel. Solid, no-frills RGB-free option with reliable timings out of the box. Good budget pick if you're upgrading gradually.

The sweet-spot kit for gaming and general multitasking in 2026 — usually sold as 2x16GB for dual-channel. Comfortable headroom for heavier browser/IDE usage or light ML work. Reliable, widely compatible XMP/EXPO profiles.

Higher-binned DDR5 kit aimed at overclockers and enthusiasts, with tighter timings and higher rated speeds than standard kits. The RGB heatspreaders add some build aesthetics too. Worth it mainly if your CPU/board can actually push the higher speeds.

A reliable, no-nonsense 32GB DDR5 kit that undercuts the premium brands while still hitting solid EXPO/XMP speeds. Good middle ground between Corsair Vengeance and the cheapest no-name kits. Popular in budget-to-midrange builds.

Crucial's own-silicon DDR5 kit — known for tight QC and compatibility since Crucial also manufactures the dies. Slightly plainer looks (no flashy heatspreaders) but very dependable. A safe pick if you just want it to work.

Budget-friendly AM5 board with WiFi 6 built in — enough VRM headroom for a Ryzen 5/7 non-X3D chip. Good starting board if you're not planning to overclock aggressively. Solid choice for a Ryzen 5 7600 based build.

A step up in VRM quality and durability (TUF = The Ultimate Force, ASUS's rugged line), suited to Ryzen 7-class CPUs including the 7800X3D. Good BIOS/UEFI experience and solid community support. A very common recommendation for AM5 mid-range builds.
Reliable mid-range AM5 board with WiFi 6E and a clean BIOS. Comparable to the ASUS TUF and MSI PRO tiers — comes down to preference/availability. Handles a Ryzen 5 or 7 comfortably.
Intel Z790 board built for 13th/14th-gen K-series CPUs with room to actually use their overclocking headroom. Strong VRM design for i7/i9-class chips. A go-to pairing for the i7-14700K in this list.

product_name: ASUS ROG Strix Z790-F Gaming WiFi
description: Premium Z790 board with ROG branding, better power delivery, and more connectivity (PCIe 5.0, multiple M.2 slots) than the Tomahawk tier. Suited for i9-class chips or anyone who wants headroom to grow into. Priced at the higher end of Z790 boards.

One of the fastest PCIe 4.0 NVMe drives available, with read/write speeds near the interface's ceiling. Great for OS + heavy application loads, large dataset work, or video editing scratch disks. Samsung's controller/firmware reliability is a big part of the appeal.

WD's gaming-focused NVMe drive — very close to the 990 Pro in real-world speed at a slightly lower price. Comes with good sustained write performance for large file transfers. A frequently recommended alternative to Samsung's flagship.

Fast PCIe 4.0 NVMe drive from Crucial with strong price-to-performance — noticeably cheaper than the Samsung/WD flagships with only a small real-world speed gap. Good pick if you want NVMe speed without paying the premium-brand tax.

A performance-tier NVMe drive that competes directly with the 990 Pro/SN850X on paper speeds, often at a friendlier price. Solid endurance rating for a boot + primary work drive. A slightly less mainstream but well-regarded option.

Samsung's budget-tier NVMe drive using a PCIe 4.0/5.0 hybrid interface — cheaper than the 990 Pro but with a real (if modest) drop in sustained speeds. Good for a secondary drive or a build where you want the Samsung name without flagship pricing.

A solid fully-modular 750W 80+ Gold PSU that comfortably powers a mid-range CPU + GPU combo like a Ryzen 5/7 with an RTX 4070-class card. Quiet under normal loads thanks to a semi-passive fan mode. A very common 'default safe choice' PSU.

850W fully-modular 80+ Gold unit with headroom for higher-end GPUs like the 4080 SUPER or 7900 XTX. Well-regarded for stable power delivery and low ripple. A step up from the RM750e for higher-wattage builds.

750W 80+ Gold PSU from Seasonic, a brand known for OEM-grade internals and long warranties. Fully modular with quiet operation — a favorite among people who prioritize PSU reliability above almost everything else. Comparable tier to the Corsair RM750e.

850W 80+ Gold PSU from be quiet!, a brand built around low-noise operation — the fan is tuned to stay near-silent under typical gaming loads. Fully modular with good build quality for the price. A strong pick if acoustics matter to you.

850W 80+ Gold PSU with native PCIe 5.0/12VHPWR connectors, useful if you're running a newer high-end GPU without an adapter cable. Fully modular and reasonably priced for the wattage. A practical choice for a 4080 SUPER or 7900 XTX build.

27-inch 1440p IPS panel with a 165Hz (overclockable to 180Hz) refresh rate — a favorite for competitive gaming without sacrificing color accuracy. Fast response times keep motion clarity solid. A well-rounded all-purpose gaming monitor.

27-inch 1440p IPS monitor from Dell's gaming line, offering strong color accuracy and a 165Hz refresh rate at a friendlier price than the LG/ASUS equivalents. Good if you split time between gaming and color-sensitive work. Solid build quality typical of Dell displays.

A long-running favorite 27-inch 1440p 165Hz IPS monitor with G-Sync compatibility and good out-of-box color. TUF branding means above-average build durability. A safe, well-reviewed pick that's been a go-to for years.

27-inch 1440p IPS monitor with a 170Hz refresh rate and a built-in KVM switch, useful if you're juggling a laptop and desktop on one screen. Generally praised for punching above its price point in color and sharpness. One of the better budget 1440p high-refresh options.

27-inch curved 1440p VA panel with a 165Hz refresh rate — VA gives deeper blacks than IPS at the cost of slightly worse viewing angles. A budget-friendly curved option for gaming-focused setups. Good if you want the curved-screen immersion without IPS pricing.
